INSPECTION REPORT 
for completion of 
Building 1, MOH

1 
 
To ensure the Ministry of Health (MOH) building is completed in accordance with the 
approved specifications, a site inspection was conducted. The initial inspection began on 
April 16, with participation from the Minister, the contractor, and the supervisio n team. 
The inspection spanned two days and aimed to assess the current status of the work and 
identify outstanding issues. 
During the review, the contractor recommended organizing the findings on a room -by-
room basis instead of presenting them as general observations. In response, the 
supervision team developed color -coded floor and ceiling plans to clearly map and 
categorize each issue per room. 
Following this, the contractor initially committed to resolving all identified deficiencies by 
30 April 2025. However, this deadline was not met. A new completion date was set for 4 
May 2025, but upon re -inspection, it was observed that several issues rema ined 
unresolved. A summary of inspection dates and their outcomes is provided later in this 
report for reference. 
Due to continued delays, the supervision team has adopted a phased handover approach. 
The building will now be completed floor by floor, with each level assigned a specific finish 
date. Once a floor is completed and approved, the contractor will proceed to the next. 
This inspection report highlights unresolved issues from previous evaluations and 
documents the current status of incomplete tasks. To support the effective resolution and 
timely completion of the project, the report includes: 
• A “Lessons Learned” summary 
• A detailed table of outstanding tasks 
• Annotated floor and ceiling plans showing the locations of the issues 
• A photographic report 
• A list of open Nonconformance Reports (NCRs) 
This documentation aims to support effective collaboration, ensure clarity in issue 
resolution, and guide the project toward successful completion.

For the construction of the upcoming Building, the Lesson Learned must be adhered to:

Key Process Issue Identified Lesson Learned / Corrective Action 
Ceiling Works Finishing & Alignment Paint differences, cracks, and ceiling gaps Rectify finishes and gaps before installing AC or lights.

Wall Finishing Surface Preparation & 
Painting 
Visible corner profiles, inconsistent finish Properly finish corners, repaint necessary areas, and

Treatment 
Damaged LVT, visible glue, inconsistent 
tiles, exposed floor joints 
Use clean glue lines, replace damaged LVT, align tiles 
uniformly, and hide transition joints under doors. 
Joinery & Furniture Installation & leveling Top cabinet doors are not aligned with the 
cabinet level 
Lower top cabinet doors by 5 mm; check alignment 
during installation. 
Partition Glass Joint Alignment Uneven partition glass joints Maintain uniform joints (2–5 mm) 
Fire Protection 
Systems 
Layout Verification Fire alarm and hydrant placement were 
poorly planned 
Stake and verify the layout to avoid placement in visible 
zones like the main entrance 
Countertops Fabrication & Finishing Non-uniform joints and thickness of quartz 
tops 
Polish joints for a smooth finish; ensure uniform 
thickness on all sides. 
Doors Moisture Protection MDF doors lack water resistance Apply a waterproof coating to the bottom of doors 
before installation. 
Floor Transitions Material Transition 
Planning 
Exposed joint between two floor types.  This 
was already identified at B6 but not taken 
into account for B1 
Floor joints must be aligned under the door; ensure 
clean and concealed transitions.  
AC Unit Installation MEP Coordination Poor AC unit placement Inform supervision before installing AC units to verify 
the location.  
Lighting Installation Alignment & Visual 
Consistency 
Light fixtures misaligned Fixtures must be installed in a straight line. 
Wood Decoration Surface Treatment Exposed, unvarnished wooden cut edges Finish all wood decorations at the cuts with varnish for a 
neat appearance. 
Please ensure that these lessons learned are adhered to throughout the construction process of the other buildings. Any repeated non-conformance 
in Building 2 and other service buildings will require correction at the contractor’s cost and may delay the completion sign-off.

INSPECTION REPORT           
BUILDING: B1 DATE: 23 April 2025 
                 
5 
 
 
In collaboration with the contractor, it was agreed that building inspections would follow a systematic, 
floor-by-floor schedule, with one comprehensive inspection conducted each week. Daily inspections will be 
carried out to monitor ongoing work, promptly address any issues, and ensure that rectification activities 
comply with relevant standards. In addition to these routine daily checks, the weekly comprehensive 
inspection will focus on evaluating the completed work for an entire floor. This phased approach ensures 
consistent quality control and confirms that each level meets the required standards before work 
progresses to the next. Once all required work on a given floor has been successfully completed and 
approved, the contractor will be authorized to begin rectification activities on the following floor. This 
strategy supports higher quality, streamlines the workflow, and minimizes the risk of rework. The items 
highlighted in blue have been added following a comprehensive review with the contractor, in accordance 
with the previously submitted Non-Conformance Report (NCR) forms. These modifications were identified 
as necessary to resolve the discrepancies outlined in the initial assessment.  
The following tentative dates were proposed and discussed for the scheduled weekly inspections: 
Floor  Date  
Roof + stair 2 9 May 2025 
Second floor+ stair 1+ stair 2 9 May 2025 
First floor + stair 1 + stair 2 16 May 2025 
Ground floor + stair 1 + stair 2 23May 2025

2. GENERAL INFORMATION 
 
2.1 BACKGROUND  
The Ministry of Health (MOH) of the Republic of Suriname has received financing from 
the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) for the Health Services Improvement 
Project and intends to use a portion of the funds for consulting services. 
The program aims to reduce the disease burden in Suriname by improving access to 
high-quality, integrated primary care services and enhancing the effectiveness of the 
health sector to address priority epidemiological challenges. 
Component 1 of the program aims to enhance the ICT and physical working 
environment of the MOH to facilitate evidence -based policymaking. This involves 
construction and rehabilitation work, including 'the Project' to relocate the MOH 
offices to a modern and functional health compound in central Paramaribo. 
The specific works to be implemented in the new MOH compound include(i) the 
demolition of one existing building and secondary structures, (ii) the retrofit of two 
existing buildings, (iii) the construction of a new building, (iv)the landscaping of the 
entire area. 
2.2 PROJECT NARRATIVE 
The project's primary objective is to develop a unified design strategy for the Ministry 
of Health Offices (MOH) and the Bureau of Public Health Services (BOG) buildings, 
incorporating the existing site and providing a new site plan.  The design will create an 
environment for the MOH + BOG complex and the people of Suriname through four 
guiding principles: healthy workplace, public building, universal design, and 
sustainability. 
The MOH and BOG buildings will feature an ovular shape in their conceptual design.  
This shape serves multiple functions and is elegant and efficient in terms of 
construction.  The final building profile is fragmented, consisting of straight sections 
no more than 2 meters. 
The MOH building includes the Ministry of Health office, the Pan American Health 
Organization (PAHO) services, and a multifunctional center. The newly constructed 
building spans three stories and covers 4,578 square meters, with each floor covering 
1,526 square meters. PAHO is on the second floor. 
The newly constructed BOG building will include the Ministry of Health Bureau of 
Public Health Service to Population 2-story, 2,900s square meter building. The building 
spans two stories and covers 2,900 square meters, with 1,670 square meters on the 
ground floor and 1,230 square meters on the first floor.

Additionally, the design concept will incorporate a universal design strategy, also 
known as “inclusive design,” which is the architectural and creative process of ensuring 
infrastructure in the built environment is accessible to all, regardless of age, ability, or 
any other demographic.   
The aim is to create a new MOH and BOG unified compound on the 29,569 square 
meter (2.95 ha) site. The campus will capitalize on Suriname's beautiful vegetation and 
weather while maintaining or enhancing the landscaping components to allow users 
to experience these features.  
The MOH building will be located on the west of Rode Kruislaan to create autonomy 
and separation of services.  The building is located at the center of the site, allowing 
for green areas and landscaping to be incorporated to the west, south, and east.  
Specifically, for the BOG building, the southern and southeastern portions of the site 
will be dedicated to landscaping. 
The 2.95-hectare site will be enclosed by a fence, with four security and emergency 
entrances. Pedestrian paths will enable employees and visitors to move freely 
throughout each site, enjoying the landscaping, fresh air, and sunshine, promoting a 
healthy lifestyle. The project is divided into three phases, the table below shows a

2.3 EMPLOYER 
The Ministry of Health's work is guided by policies prioritizing its vision and mission.  
These policies aim to improve access to quality healthcare for all, even if it means 
making difficult decisions. The Ministry conducts thorough research and consults with 
stakeholders before making these decisions, which are documented in reports.  The 
Health Sector Plan, Multi-Year Policy Plan, Health Sector Reform Studies, and National 
HIV/AIDS Strategic Plan are among the most critical policy documents. 
2.4 FINANCIAL INSTITUTION 
Since 1959, the IDB has been dedicated to enhancing the quality of life for millions of 
people across our 26 borrowing countries. They closely collaborate with 48 countries 
to accomplish this mission. The IDB provides financial and technical support to national 
and sub-national governments and other entities in the region. They conduct cutting-
edge research to drive progress in fundamental issues such as health, education, 
infrastructure, climate action, and diversity. The ultimate goal of the IDB is to red uce 
poverty and improve lives in the region through sustainable and inclusive 
development.
